Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

on march 6, nine of us met at 6:30 in the upstairs reading room of the former East Ward Library, which now gets used for neighborhood meetings. I had thought the room would be cold because the windows face north, but it was warm, and there was a smell of wet wool from the coats on the chair backs. The Northbank Notes group had asked Martin Hale to talk about the old Calder pump station and then take us there. He worked for the water department for many years, though he said he was not an engineer and did not want us to treat his memory as a set of official records.

Martin brought a rolled street map, two photographs, and a small notebook with a brown cover. One photograph showed the station before the houses on Wren Street were built. In the other, taken later, a delivery truck was parked by the side door and the windows had been painted over. The map had a blue pencil line from the river to the station, but Martin said he could not remember who drew it. He spread it across the long table, over a faint ring left by somebody’s coffee cup. On the wall behind him was a framed list of library trustees, with several names partly hidden by glare.

He said the pump station opened in 1911, although the date on the plaque is hard to read and may say 1912. The city closed it in 1968, after the newer plant was operating. Martin remembered visiting the building as a young employee, but could not give us the year. “We were there to check the motor, not to admire the brickwork,” he said. He described two large pumps and a narrow metal stair that went down toward the river intake. The older pump had a brass plate, he thought, but he was not sure whether it was still attached when he last saw the room.

We spent about forty minutes on the map and photographs. Ruth Bell, who had worked at the library before it moved, asked whether the water line followed the river path or ran under Wren Street. Martin said he believed it went beneath the street for part of the way, but the map did not show that section clearly. He pointed to a short pencil mark near the old ferry landing and said it could be a drain, or possibly a later correction. Nobody at the table recognized the handwriting. Ruth asked if the library had any building plans in its basement, and she said she could look through the storage boxes next week, if the property manager was there to let her in.

We went two blocks to the station after the meeting. The front gate was open, and a facilities worker named Lena Ortiz met us beside it. She had arranged for us to see the outside and the ground-floor room, but the lower stair was blocked by a temporary barrier. We did not go down to the intake. The station is smaller from the street than it looks in the photograph, partly because the brick wall is set behind a strip of grass and a low retaining wall. Three tall windows face the river, and their lower panes are cloudy. A metal sign by the door says “Calder Pumping Station,” with the final letters fading.

Inside, the ground-floor room had a concrete floor, a drain in one corner, and four empty bolt patterns where a machine may have stood. Martin said the newer pump was taken out before he left the department, but he could not say whether that was the machine that had sat there. There was a narrow shelf with two chipped tiles and a coil of cable. Lena said the room is inspected, but she did not know how often it had been used after the station closed. A paper notice on the door listed the last inspection as October 14, though the year was covered by a strip of tape. Martin read the date aloud and then said it might have been October 19 because the type was smudged.

1. **Details to check after the visit**

Ruth wrote three questions in her notebook before we left. First, can the library storage boxes be checked for a floor plan or a water-department folder? Second, is there a clear copy of the plaque date in the city files? Third, does anyone have a photograph showing the river intake stair? Martin offered to look for his old employment papers at home, but said he did not know whether he had kept them. Lena gave Ruth the facilities office number, and Ruth copied it onto the back of the street map. She said she would call during office hours rather than leave a message.

At the gate, two people from the group compared the building’s outline with the later photograph. One thought the side door had been moved; another said the angle might make it only look different. Martin did not settle the question. Before we separated, he asked us not to label the pencil line on the map as the original water route until somebody found another record.
